statement: Show that, for $0<x<\pi$, $\dfrac{\sin3x}{\sin x}=2\cos2x+1$. Hence solve the equation $\sin3x=\sin x$ for $0<x<2\pi$.
solution: $\sin3x=\sin x(3-4\sin^{2}x)=\sin x(4\cos^{2}x-1)=\sin x(2\cos2x+1)$, so the identity holds. Then $\sin3x=\sin x$ gives either $\sin x=0$ (so $x=\pi$ in the interval) or $2\cos2x+1=1$, i.e. $\cos2x=0$, giving $2x=\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{3\pi}{2},\tfrac{5\pi}{2},\tfrac{7\pi}{2}$, so $x=\tfrac{\pi}{4},\tfrac{3\pi}{4},\tfrac{5\pi}{4},\tfrac{7\pi}{4}$. The full solution set is $x=\tfrac{\pi}{4},\tfrac{3\pi}{4},\pi,\tfrac{5\pi}{4},\tfrac{7\pi}{4}$.
hints: Express $\sin3x$ in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
Factor the equation into $\sin x=0$ and $2\cos2x+1=1$.
